design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA-guided; no protocol or registration mentioned) of the psychiatric symptom profile and the duration of methamphetamine-associated psychosis across all designs: 94 studies with 7387 participants (20 cross-sectional, 29 case-control, 10 longitudinal, 29 case reports with 49 cases, 6 laboratory studies in which methamphetamine was given to induce psychotic symptoms). Each study was reduced to symptom present or absent; persistence was the share of participants with symptoms more than one month after stopping use, summarized as unweighted medians across studies. Read: the cover sheet and all article pages of the online-first PDF (pp. 1–11, pages numbered as printed on that version); Figures 1 and 2 are images whose values are given in the text; Supplementary Tables S1 to S7 not read.
can_establish: Which psychiatric symptoms the published literature on methamphetamine-associated psychosis reports, and how often studies report them, up to March 2018; and the spread across studies of the share still psychotic after a month and of later schizophrenia diagnoses.
cannot_establish: A pooled or population rate of persistence or of transition to schizophrenia (unweighted medians of study proportions, no intervals, no appraisal of study quality); how frequent or severe any symptom is (binary coding of studies); persistence in people who are never hospitalized (no community study of duration); and whether methamphetamine causes lasting psychosis or reveals a primary psychotic illness.

sample.recruitment: PsycINFO, Medline, PubMed, Scopus and Ovid searched with a librarian to 14 March 2018, plus hand-searching of recent issues of key journals, subject reviews and reference lists: 4455 records (4451 from databases, 4 by hand), 2464 after de-duplication, 404 full texts (pp. 2–3). Included studies were published 1949 to 2018; 72% recruited hospital in- or outpatients, 11% drug-treatment services, 5% prisons, 4% community settings and 3% private practitioners (p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English-language empirical studies in humans of the profile or duration of symptoms in people whom the authors identified as having symptoms of methamphetamine-associated psychosis, who were diagnosed with it, or who had substance-induced psychosis and currently used methamphetamine or amphetamine. Excluded: reviews, commentaries, unpublished papers and book chapters; where several articles described one population only the most detailed was kept (15 excluded) (pp. 2–3).
sample.demographics: Mostly men (interquartile range of study percentages 70–90%); mean ages 29 to 37 years (interquartile range); 45% of studies reported the share with methamphetamine dependence, median 99% where reported. Substance of interest: methamphetamine in 59 studies (63%), amphetamine 15 (16%), both 8 (9%), prescription amphetamines 30 (32%) (p. 4).
sample.attrition: Longitudinal studies followed participants for 3 months to 16 years and retained 54–100% (interquartile range) (p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Weighted to hospitalized, mostly male samples with dependence; the authors note that this may overstate negative and understate affective symptoms, and that people with milder or transient symptoms who do not seek care are missed (p. 8). English-language, published studies only.

exposure.measurement: As defined by each study: an explicit diagnosis of methamphetamine-associated or substance-induced psychosis in 65% of studies (DSM in 23, ICD in 9, both in 5, the Chinese CCMD-3 in 1), and otherwise identification of symptoms by the study's authors; standardized symptom scales in 4% of case reports and in 40% to 80% of the other designs (p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized; the authors note that many included studies did not account for frequency or duration of use (p. 8). Laboratory studies gave methamphetamine under study conditions, once or repeatedly over hours or days (p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled; the authors list polydrug use among the factors most included studies did not adjust for (p. 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Persistence was counted from cessation of use as each study reported it; verification of abstinence is not described, and the authors note that no study measured duration in community samples, probably because abstinence is hard to verify there (p. 8).

comparison.controls: None for the descriptive synthesis; from case-control studies only the data on participants with methamphetamine-associated psychosis were used (p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, earlier psychotic episodes and premorbid functioning are not synthesized, so persistent cases cannot be separated from primary psychoses.

outcomes.instruments: Whatever each study used: BPRS (9 studies), PANSS (3), MINI (3), SANS (3), SAPS (2), Methamphetamine Experience Questionnaire (2), SCID (2), CIDI (1), or case descriptions (pp. 4–5).
outcomes.operationalization: Symptom present (reported as a prevalence, a scale score or in a case description) or absent; persistence as symptoms continuing more than one month after stopping use, the DSM-5 time frame; for case reports, time to resolution in bands (one week or less, 1–4 weeks, 1–6 months, over 6 months); for laboratory studies, the longest time to resolution (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the descriptive tallies of about 30 symptoms (Figure 2, Table 1); the one significance test (Japanese versus other studies, p. 6) is uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Eligibility: one reviewer judged all 404 full texts and a second independently judged 336 (85%), with 88% initial agreement and 42 disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer (p. 3); extraction by one reviewer, the first author taking responsibility for its accuracy (p. 9).

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or intervals. Share of studies reporting each symptom: persecutory delusions 84%, auditory hallucinations 69%, visual hallucinations 65%, hostility 53%, conceptual disorganization 36%, depression 31%, flat affect 19%, other negative symptoms 6–15% (p. 5). Persistence beyond one month (27 studies): median 25%; longitudinal studies median 40% (range 14–96%); laboratory studies none (resolution within 12 hours to 7 days); Japanese studies median 44% (18–96%) against 12% (0–39%) elsewhere, t = 4.79, p = .0001; case reports 2 of 24 (8%) (p. 6). Later schizophrenia diagnosis: 33–38% after 6–7 years in two studies, 16% within 16 years in one (p. 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; a PRISMA checklist is in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Duration was extracted only where a proportion with persistence could be calculated (27 of 94 studies); the median includes six laboratory studies in which persistence was impossible by design, and only 25 of the 27 studies are accounted for in the comparison by country.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the t-test (degrees of freedom not reported) compares study-level proportions from 11 Japanese and 14 other studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 27 studies with duration data, the median study reported 25% of participants still psychotic more than a month after stopping use, with a range from none (laboratory administration to volunteers) to 96%, higher in Japanese studies (median 44%) than elsewhere (12%); two cohorts found a third or more re-diagnosed with schizophrenia after 6–7 years and a Finnish register study 16% within 16 years. The symptom profile is a tally of how many studies reported each symptom.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives the median of 25% for persistence beyond one month without saying that it is an unweighted median of study proportions spanning 0% to 96% that includes laboratory studies with no possible persistence, and concludes that negative symptoms "are typically absent" (p. 1) from the share of studies reporting them, a binary tally that the authors themselves say cannot give prevalence (p. 9). The suggestion that persistent psychosis may be drug-precipitated schizophrenia is offered as a hypothesis needing research (p. 8). The abstract counts 20 longitudinal studies where the results count 10 (reporting issue 1).

timeline.event: Narrative review on whether amphetamine psychosis is a separate entity or a primary psychosis triggered in vulnerable people (Bramness et al., 2012), cited by this review.
Narrative review giving 16% and 17% still psychotic after 1 and 3 months of abstinence (Glasner-Edwards & Mooney, 2014).
Systematic review of risk factors for methamphetamine-associated psychosis from an overlapping author group (Arunogiri et al., 2018), cited by this review.
Narrative review of methamphetamine psychosis compared with schizophrenia (Wearne & Cornish, 2018).
This review: the first systematic review of the symptom profile, duration and course, by the authors' account (p. 7).
Meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced, brief and atypical psychoses to schizophrenia (Murrie et al., 2020); identified by the currency check of 2026-10-16, not yet read.
A meta-analysis of methamphetamine psychosis versus schizophrenia cites this review for the rarity of negative symptoms (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024, p. 188).

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review of duration identified so far. Its persistence figure is a crude unweighted median and its transition figures are quoted from three studies, none appraised. It is best cited for the range of reported persistence and for the Japanese excess with its likely diagnostic explanation; pooled transition rates should come from the 2020 meta-analysis and the register cohorts once read.

funding.funder: Australian Postgraduate Scholarship held by the first author (p. 9).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: Australian National University; National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; St Vincent's Hospital and the University of Melbourne; Curtin University. The senior author (McKetin) is an author of several studies the review cites (McKetin et al., 2016a, 2016b, 2017); whether they are among the included studies is shown only in a supplement not read, and no procedure for appraising one's own studies is described.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective inception cohort of people presenting with methamphetamine psychosis in emergency and community settings, with urine-verified abstinence, structured diagnostic reassessment at 1, 6 and 12 months and after several years, family history and premorbid functioning recorded at entry and antipsychotic treatment documented, reporting with confidence intervals the share still psychotic and the share later diagnosed with a primary psychosis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: A descriptive question: population (people identified with methamphetamine-associated psychosis) and outcomes (symptom profile, duration) are specified; no comparator is needed (pp. 2–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
All designs from case reports to laboratory studies were included without an explanation of the choice; the descriptive question would justify it, but none is given.

Five sources searched with a librarian and an example Medline strategy given, plus hand-searching of journals, reviews and reference lists (pp. 2–3); but Ovid is a platform hosting Medline and PsycINFO rather than a separate database, the search was limited to English-language published studies without justification, and no grey literature or registries were searched. 'Partial yes' as in the project's other review cards; a strict reading of the unjustified language restriction would give 'no'.

A second reviewer independently judged 85% of full texts with 88% initial agreement (p. 3), which meets AMSTAR 2's option of duplicate selection of a sample with at least 80% agreement; abstract screening is not described as duplicate.
Extraction by one reviewer; no second extractor is described (p. 9).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for exclusion appear only as counts in the PRISMA figure; the supplements the article describes (S1 to S7) list included studies only.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: per-study characteristics are only in Supplementary Tables S3 to S7, which were not read; the article itself describes the included studies only in aggregate.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the included studies; the authors note that studies of disparate quality were aggregated without weighting (p. 9).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: No meta-analysis; unweighted medians of study proportions and one t-test.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: No study-level risk of bias was assessed, so none could be accounted for; the discussion names design-level limitations of the reviewed studies (hospital samples, self-report, no adjustment for polydrug use or medication, laboratory confinement) (p. 8).
Variation by design, country, diagnostic system, sex ratio and recruitment setting is described and discussed, including the diagnostic explanation of the Japanese excess (pp. 6, 8).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (a postgraduate scholarship) and the absence of conflicts are stated (p. 9).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2: no protocol; 7: no list of excluded studies; 9: no appraisal of the included studies; 13: risk of bias therefore not accounted for) and item 4 is only partly met: critically low confidence; the provisional item 8 cannot change this. The review is a careful descriptive tally and may be cited for which symptoms and what range of persistence the literature reports; its median persistence and transition figures are unappraised second-hand summaries and should not be cited as rates.

key_findings.finding: Searches to 14 March 2018 plus hand-searching gave 4455 records, 2464 screened and 404 full texts; 94 studies with 7387 participants were included: 20 cross-sectional, 29 case-control, 10 longitudinal, 29 case reports (49 cases) and 6 laboratory administration studies, published 1949 to 2018.
key_findings.locator: Method › Search strategy (pp. 2–3); Inclusion criteria (p. 3); Results › Study characteristics › Overview of studies (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 20 longitudinal studies; the results give 10, which with the other designs sums to 94.

key_findings.finding: 72% of studies recruited hospital in- or outpatients; samples were mostly men (interquartile range 70–90%) with mean ages of 29 to 37 years; only 65% of studies gave an explicit diagnosis of methamphetamine-associated or substance-induced psychosis (18% of case reports, none of the laboratory studies).
key_findings.locator: Results › Participant demographics; Diagnosis or identification of MAP

key_findings.finding: Share of studies reporting each symptom: persecutory delusions 84%, auditory hallucinations 69%, visual hallucinations 65%, hostility 53%, conceptual disorganization 36%, depression 31%, hyperactivity 28%, tactile hallucinations 21%, flat affect 19%, other negative symptoms 6–15%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Profile of psychiatric symptoms; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Shares of studies reporting a symptom, not shares of people; each study was coded only as symptom present or absent.

key_findings.finding: 27 studies (12 case-control, 5 cross-sectional, 4 longitudinal, 6 laboratory) gave the share of participants with psychotic symptoms more than one month after stopping use: median 25%. No laboratory study found persistence (symptoms abated within 12 hours to 7 days of the last dose); longitudinal studies reported a median of 40% (range 14–96%).

Japanese studies (11 of the 27, 41%) reported a median of 44% persisting (range 18–96%), against 12% (range 0–39%) in 14 studies from the USA, Australia, Canada, Iran and elsewhere in Asia (t = 4.79, p = .0001). Japanese studies more often used ICD-10 (35%) than DSM-IV (25%), the others mostly DSM-IV (42%, ICD-10 6%); the discussion attributes the excess to the ICD classification, under which psychosis may last up to 6 months after intoxication before a primary psychotic disorder is diagnosed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Duration of symptoms, 2nd paragraph (p. 6); Discussion › Duration of psychotic symptoms, 1st paragraph (pp. 7–8)
key_findings.note: 11 plus 14 is 25 of the 27 studies; the other two are not described.

key_findings.finding: Of 24 case reports giving duration, symptoms persisted beyond one month in 2 (8%), lasted 1–4 weeks in 14 (58%) and one week or less in 8 (printed as 36%).

Four longitudinal studies tracked symptoms over time: positive symptoms fell in three and were stable in one; negative symptoms were stable in three and rose in one (Tomiyama 1990, hospitalized patients on antipsychotics, over 4 months); in a 3-month follow-up (Javadian 2016) positive symptoms rose in those who resumed methamphetamine use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three longitudinal studies reported later schizophrenia diagnoses: 33–38% re-diagnosed after 6–7 years in two (Kittirattanapaiboon et al., 2010, 1116 people; Medhus et al., 2015, 28 people) and 16% within 16 years in a study of 825 people (Niemi-Pynttäri et al., 2013).
key_findings.locator: Results › Longitudinal changes in symptom profile, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The review writes these sample sizes with k, its symbol for numbers of studies; they are numbers of people. The Finnish study's title describes a register of 18,478 inpatient cases of substance-induced psychosis (reference list, p. 11).

key_findings.finding: Of 104 psychiatric inpatients with amphetamine delusional disorder who did not meet criteria for schizophrenia (Iwanami et al., 1994), 27% had symptoms beyond one month and 17% beyond three months despite abstinence and antipsychotic treatment.

The authors state that many included studies did not adjust for polydrug use, frequency and duration of use or antipsychotic medication; that most recruited inpatients and may reflect more severe illness; that no study examined duration in community samples; and that binary coding cannot give prevalence and studies were not weighted for quality or size.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the reviewed studies, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 8); Limitations of the current review (p. 9)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract counts 20 longitudinal studies; the results count 10, and only 10 makes the designs sum to the 94 studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the results' count is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The substance categories add up to 112 studies (120%): methamphetamine 59, amphetamine 15, both 8, prescription amphetamines 30, out of 94.
reporting_issues.consequence: The categories overlap or a count is wrong; how many studies concern methamphetamine alone cannot be read off.

reporting_issues.issue: Case reports with symptoms lasting one week or less are given as 8 of 24 (36%); 8 of 24 is 33%.
The sample sizes of the transition studies are written with k (1116, 28), the review's symbol for numbers of studies elsewhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Could be misread as numbers of studies; they are people.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison by country accounts for 25 of the 27 studies with duration data (11 Japanese, 14 others), and the median of 25% includes six laboratory studies in which persistence was impossible by design; the median without them is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 25% understates the median among clinical studies by an unknown amount and cannot be recomputed without the supplement.
